questions.learningObjective: Explain how a president acquired foreign territory under existing constitutional powers.
questions.stem: A memo asks you to explain how a president could acquire foreign territory without any amendment to the constitution.

answer.exemplar: The administration relied on powers the constitution already granted, especially the power to make treaties and the power to guarantee a republican form of government against foreign interference, and treated the acquisition as a treaty matter signed with the foreign government rather than a new act of legislation. Territory already governed by the United States had been admitted on that reasoning before, and the government took the position that the nation could acquire new territory by the same means and later organize it through ordinary legislation under the territorial system.

questions.explanation: The question asks for the constitutional reasoning rather than a chronology. A strong answer names the treaty power, the guarantee clause, and the precedent of earlier territorial acquisitions.
questions.hint: Name the clause and the precedent relied on.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the territorial system made a distant region governable.
questions.stem: A planner's memo asks you to explain how the territorial system made a distant region governable.

answer.exemplar: The system turned an unsettled district into a step toward statehood by fixing in advance what each stage of self-government required: first a governor, a judge and a legislature with limited authority, then a legislature able to pass its own laws over the governor's veto, and finally enough population to petition for admission as a state. Because the rules were written before the settlers arrived, administrators had a standard to apply, and the promises of schools, religious freedom and civil rights gave emigrants a reason to settle. The system also kept federal law and federal land policy in place while the region matured.

questions.explanation: The question asks how the stages gave both a standard and an incentive. A strong answer explains the graduated authority and the accompanying guarantees that encouraged settlement.
questions.hint: Mention both the graduated authority and the inducements.

questions.stem: A memo asks you to explain why the outgoing president's last-hour actions were disputed by the incoming one.

answer.exemplar: In the final hours of his term the outgoing president signed a law creating new federal judgeships and attached riders to it, and he used the power of appointment to fill those seats and other offices with loyal supporters. questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why contemporaries treated 1801 as a turning point.
questions.stem: A planner's memo asks you to explain why contemporaries treated 1801 as a turning point rather than an ordinary election.

answer.exemplar: Two things were unusual at once. An opposition party that had spent years in opposition took the presidency, the vice presidency and control of Congress, and the change happened without any appeal to arms, with outgoing officials still in office and even some of them voting for the incoming candidate. That combination, a revolution in the party system carried out through the ordinary forms of law, convinced contemporaries that the republic could survive an alternation of power, and it also convinced them that the new party would now use that opening to reshape the government it had inherited.

questions.explanation: The question asks for the features contemporaries emphasised. A strong answer names the party change, the absence of force, and the expectation of a new programme.
questions.hint: Point to both the change of party and the absence of force.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a change in counting electoral votes was thought necessary.
questions.stem: A planner's memo asks you to explain why a change in the counting of electoral votes was thought necessary after 1800.

answer.exemplar: Before the change, each elector cast two votes with no designation of office, so the candidate with the second-highest total automatically became vice president. When the two leading candidates for president tied in electoral votes, the House had to choose among them, and because each state delegation cast a single vote, a deadlock of many ballots followed that could be broken only by a member of the losing side. The separate ballot removed the automatic runner-up, allowed the House to pick from three candidates when electors failed to agree, and left the Senate to choose a vice president from the top two.

questions.explanation: The question asks for a chain of causes from the old rules to the new ones. A strong answer links the undifferentiated ballot to the tie, the chamber deadlock and then the reforms.
questions.hint: Start from the old two-vote rule and follow the consequences.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a rider can change the character of a measure.
questions.stem: A memo asks you to explain how a rider attached to a bill could change the character of a law.

answer.exemplar: A rider is a provision carried along with a measure on which the vote turns, and it can be used to carry a subject that would not survive on its own. In 1801 a rider was used to add new federal judgeships to a routine reorganization of the courts, so that a modest administrative bill became the vehicle for a permanent enlargement of the judiciary. Because the rider took effect with the larger measure and was pushed through in the final hours of a term, it gave the outgoing president a way to shape the courts that the incoming administration would have to work within.

questions.explanation: The question asks for a general principle and then its application. A strong answer defines the rider and explains how it carried a larger change under cover of a minor measure.
questions.hint: Define the device first, then apply it to the courts.

questions.learningObjective: Trace the journey of the expedition from the Mississippi to the Pacific and back.

stimulus.body: An abstract of the expedition's journal records the party leaving the Mississippi in the spring of 1804 with boats, mules, guns and stores, wintering among the Mandan villages in the far north, climbing to the high passes of the mountains with the help of Shoshone guides, and descending by the end of the following year to a broad river whose mouth opens on the western ocean. The journal notes that the party then turned back and reached home in the autumn of 1806.

questions.stem: A planner's memo quotes an abstract of the expedition's journal; the reader says the party reached the Atlantic; what does the abstract show?

options.text: That the party never left the Mississippi and the mountains were never crossed

options.text: That the party travelled to the western ocean and then turned back to return home
That the party crossed the Atlantic by ship and never saw the mountains
options.misconception: Invents an Atlantic crossing by sea

options.text: That the party reached the western ocean and then sailed on to Europe
options.misconception: Extends the voyage beyond the return to America

questions.explanation: The journal describes a journey to the Pacific and a return the following autumn, with a winter in the north and a crossing of the mountains. The errors stop the journey early or carry it out of the hemisphere.
questions.hint: Note which ocean the river mouth opens on.

questions.learningObjective: Analyze the mixture of change and continuity in the 1801 transfer.

stimulus.body: A planner's note records that the incoming administration took office with the same ministers of the department he had criticized, that the judges who had been appointed in the final hours were never seated, and that the outgoing party remained a force in the legislature. questions.hint: Weigh the change in officeholders against the continuity of men.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the last-hour measures became a lasting example in arguments about power.
questions.stem: A memo asks you to explain why the last-hour measures became a lasting example in arguments about executive power.

answer.exemplar: The episode supplied a memorable test for a persistent question: how far could a president go in shaping the government in the days before his successor took the oath. Because the acts were few, dated, and made in the open, they could be named, repeated and attacked, and the incoming president's refusal to seal the commissions turned the controversy into a test case of his own doctrine. Later arguments about the removal of officers, about the length of a term, and about the limits of patronage all borrowed the vocabulary that this first quarrel established.

questions.explanation: The question asks why the episode endured as a precedent. A strong answer explains that it produced clear facts, a test case, and a vocabulary later disputes could reuse.
questions.hint: Explain what made the episode usable in later arguments.
